column1: What fundamental right/obligation asymmetry distinguishes options from futures/forwards?
column2: Options give the buyer the right but not the obligation to transact at a predetermined price; futures/forwards impose symmetric obligations on both counterparties.

column1: How is an option's premium decomposed, and how does each component behave over time?
column2: Premium = Intrinsic Value + Time Value. Intrinsic value moves linearly/deterministically with spot price; time value decays continuously toward zero as expiration approaches (theta decay), collapsing to zero on expiration day.

column1: Define moneyness for calls vs. puts in terms of spot (S) and strike (K).
column2: Call: ITM when S > K, ATM when S = K, OTM when S < K. Put: ITM when K > S, ATM when S = K, OTM when K < S (inverted relative to calls).

column1: What is the single inviolable principle underlying all arbitrage-free derivatives pricing?
column2: The Law of One Price: if two portfolios produce identical cash flows in every future state, they must have identical present values today, or a riskless arbitrage profit is available.

column1: In the binomial option pricing model, what does the replicating portfolio consist of, and why does it eliminate the need for true probability estimates?
column2: It consists of Δ shares of the underlying asset and B dollars in a risk-free bond, constructed to exactly match the option's payoff in both the up and down states. Since it replicates payoffs under arbitrage-free pricing, only the no-arbitrage condition is needed—not the real-world probabilities of up/down moves.

column1: What does Delta measure, and what does Gamma measure relative to Delta?
column2: Delta measures the rate of change of option value with respect to the underlying asset's price (first-order sensitivity). Gamma measures the rate of change of Delta itself as the underlying moves (second-order sensitivity, i.e., curvature).

column1: What are the five primary Greeks in the Black-Scholes framework and what risk factor does each isolate?
column2: Delta (underlying price), Gamma (curvature/rate of change of Delta), Theta (time decay), Vega (implied volatility), Rho (interest rate changes).

column1: What is the characteristic Greek signature of a long option position vs. a short option position?
column2: Long options: positive Gamma, negative Theta (pay time decay for convexity). Short options: negative Gamma, positive Theta (collect time decay but exposed to adverse convexity moves).

column1: What is the volatility smile/skew, and what does it reveal about the Black-Scholes model's core assumption?
column2: The smile/skew is the empirical pattern where implied volatility varies by strike (typically decreasing as strike increases for equity index options—negative skew). It reveals that Black-Scholes' assumption of constant volatility (homoscedasticity) is violated, and the true return distribution exhibits negative skewness and excess kurtosis.

column1: In a bull call debit spread (long call at K1, short call at K2, K2 > K1, same expiration), what are the maximum profit and maximum loss?
column2: Maximum profit = (K2 - K1) - net premium paid. Maximum loss = net premium paid.

column1: What three fundamental forces determine the bid-ask spread in options market microstructure?
column2: Adverse selection risk (fear of trading against informed counterparties), inventory management costs (cost of delta-hedging accumulated positions), and capital constraints (VaR limits and margin requirements imposed by clearing brokers/exchanges).

column1: Why are implied volatility and bid-ask spreads highly correlated in options markets?
column2: Higher volatility makes delta-hedging more difficult and expensive for market makers, raising their inventory management costs, which they pass on by widening bid-ask spreads.
